decisions.reason: Despite its disappearance from later website snapshots, this 2018 airfield-control launch carries substantial engineering investment, was publicly framed as setting a new standard, and is close to the firm's core integrated-airfield strategy, so management would still tend to continue it.

This surveillance display supports the firm's real-time integrated operations direction and likely benefited from meaningful development work, but the weaker public commitment and later non-observation make it somewhat easier to discontinue than A.

The training program is less capital-intensive and easier to reshape than hardware or software products, yet it complements the firm's installed systems and service model, which makes management somewhat inclined to retain it rather than admit a misstep.

As a narrower training course with limited sunk cost, low public visibility and weaker strategic centrality, this is the kind of offering management can most readily remove or fold into other services.

An airport collaboration software tool sits squarely in the firm's stated move toward collaborative, data-driven and integrated airport operations, so prior development effort and strategic relevance strongly favor continuation.

Because this multilateration system was presented as a flagship technology and fits the firm's future-facing surveillance and automation agenda, high sunk cost and strong public commitment make management very reluctant to withdraw it.
